source.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
source.authors: Jing Huang; Atticus Geiger; Karel D'Oosterlinck; Zhengxuan Wu; Christopher Potts

record.file_problem: The text is substantially complete. Some table formatting is flattened, so values that cannot be confidently assigned to individual probe sizes are not extracted.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly evaluates whether neuron explanations predict activations on test sentences and whether they have causal efficacy. Its observational results show substantial errors even for explanations with high GPT-4 scores, refining the claim that neuron explanations are faithful.
record.gate_note: The observational evaluation directly bears on V6 and V7. The intervention results assess causal mediation, not the activation-prediction behavior specified by those versions; they are not included as rows. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study checks GPT-4 explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons, which already have high simulation scores (≥0.8), against new test sentences. They predict activations poorly (F1 0.56), which bears directly on V6. It does not measure what share of neurons gets good simulation scores, so V7 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. GPT-4 explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons show low observational F1 (precision 0.64, recall 0.50) even for top-scoring neurons, and little or no causal efficacy. The authors question natural language as the explanation medium and neurons as the unit of analysis, and prefer structured formalisms and groups of neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The study audits GPT-4-generated GPT-2 XL neuron explanations using observational tests on constructed test sentences and causal interventions; it does not reproduce the explanation-generation method itself.
record.method_sensitivity: Observational precision differs for form-based versus other explanations. F1 rises when learned probes aggregate more neurons, while the margin over the random baseline decreases.

fits_no_version.finding: In interchange interventions, neurons picked by GPT-4 explanations give IIA about equal to randomly picked neurons on most tasks, far below the token-activation correlation baseline. No single-neuron intervention changed behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons named by natural-language explanations are not causal mediators of the explained concept, beyond what random neuron selection gives.

record.peer_reviewed: BlackboxNLP Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
record.problems: The observational audit samples 300 explanations from a subset of 1.7k high-scoring explanations and uses GPT-3.5-generated test material, with manual checks and exclusions. The study primarily concerns one pretrained model, GPT-2 XL. No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are stated for the extracted observational metrics.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 contains additional probe-size values, but the extracted layout does not reliably associate all values with their columns; the prose-stated learned-probe F1 and trend are retained in r4. Intervention-evaluation results are not included because they assess causal mediation rather than the activation-prediction behavior named by the tested versions.

untested.parts: No pole-share audit, and no Qwen3-32B.
No comparison of shares across models or scale.
No vision neurons and no test of the InceptionV1 cat/car example.
No comparison across architectures or tools, and no interpretable-share estimates.
No attribution graphs or replacement models.
Only GPT-4 explanations of one model, GPT-2 XL. Inspection by humans is not tested.
The share of neurons getting good simulation scores is not measured, and explainer strength is not varied. The 1.7k-of-300K (0.6%) figure is a selection value taken from Bills et al.

missing.what: Table 1 probe results for N=1/2/4/16 against the random baseline. Some values are readable: GPT-4 0.67/0.60/0.64/0.73 vs random 0.54/0.29/0.44/0.69, but the column assignment is uncertain.
Qualitative finding that most Type II errors are activations on unrelated but coherent concepts. Example: a days-of-week neuron fires on 'on Google'.
Analytic argument that an explanation with precision 0.50 can still get a perfect GPT-4 simulation score, because the 10-example scoring is insensitive to Type I errors.

record.verdict_notes: Bills et al. is an original source for V7, but this study is not, so verdicts are allowed here. V7 is left untested because the study only uses simulation scores to select neurons and never reports the share of neurons scoring well. The study's evidence is that even high scores overstate faithfulness, which fits V6 rather than V7. Test sets were generated by GPT-3.5 and manually verified (over 95% valid). No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not estimate the share of neuron poles with one or two jobs or the share not understood, and it does not study Qwen3-32B.
No cross-model or model-scale comparison of shares of interpretable neuron poles is reported.
The study does not test the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, or recursive generalization.
The study does not compare architectures, regularization, tools, or interpretability shares in vision models.
The study does not evaluate attribution graphs or compare them with trained replacement models or reconstruction error.
The observational test concerns GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons, not audits of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or a broad range of models.
The study evaluates GPT-4-generated explanations on GPT-2 XL; it does not compare multiple explainer models or estimate the share of all neurons meeting a defined good-score threshold.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 XL single neurons with GPT-4 explanations scored ≥0.8, tested on new sentences
relationships.reason: High-scoring explanations still mispredict firing: F1 0.56, precision 0.64, recall 0.50, and score–F1 correlation −0.1. Neurons also fire on antonyms and unrelated concepts (r1, r2, r3, r5, r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: Even these high-scoring explanations mispredicted firing, with F1 0.56, precision 0.64 and recall 0.50, and the explanation score correlated with F1 at only −0.1. Neurons also fired on antonyms and unrelated concepts.

tranche.reason: Gives results (P 0.64, R 0.50, IIA ≈ random) and an explicit argument that single-neuron NL explanations are unfaithful and neurons may not be the right unit, i.e. that 'neurons are already clean' needs restating. T5 fits; T2 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: The 0.56/0.64/0.50 figures are for single neurons with no probe, on explanations with GPT-4 score >=0.8 (top 0.6%); with probes F1 is 0.60. Precision sentences are written by GPT-3.5; the recall set is corpus sentences where the neuron fires, labelled by GPT-3.5. No uncertainty is reported. The intervention result (GPT-4-picked neurons give IIA ≈ random) has no row. V7 is not tested.

statements.problem: All numbers for this study match: 300 (18%) of 1.7k, F1 0.56, random 0, precision 0.64, recall 0.50, correlation -0.1, 0.62, at least 6 antonym cases. Minor: the 100 are explanations with Type II errors, not 100 error cases.

statements.correction: Appendix B: form-based explanations have precision 0.78 and the rest 0.62 (22% vs 38% of predicted-firing strings do not fire). Recall by explanation type is not reported. Form-based membership was checked by regex. Failure is present in both groups, so this supports V6 rather than limiting it.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the item is filed as limits_scope/against V6. At precision 0.78, 22% of predicted firings still fail. Only precision (Type I) is split by explanation type, so 'predictive failure is smaller' covers false positives only.

Precision 0.64 and recall 0.50 for score >=0.8 explanations are right, and so is the GPT-3.5 test material. 'GPT-4 working from 5 top excerpts' is not in this text, which gives 5 top + 5 random only for computing the GPT-4 score. That detail rests on Bills.

statements.correction: Form-based precision 0.78 vs 0.62 for the rest (Appendix B). Failure is present in both groups (22% vs 38% false positives), and recall by type is not reported. This supports V6 in both groups.
statements.problem: The numbers and the IIA ≈ random claim (Section 4.4) are right. But 'Limits_scope:' frames the form-based split as qualifying V6, when failure is still present (precision 0.78) and only precision is split by type.
